content: Edwards syndrome, also known as Trisomy 18, is a genetic disorder characterized by the presence of an extra copy of chromosome 18 in a person’s cells, instead of the usual two copies. This condition leads to significant intellectual disability and abnormalities in various parts of the body. Individuals with Trisomy 18 often exhibit low birth weight, a small and abnormally shaped head, a small jaw and mouth, clenched fists with overlapping fingers, heart defects, and abnormalities in other organs. Due to the presence of multiple life-threatening medical complications, many infants with Trisomy 18 do not survive beyond their first month of life. Only 5% to 10% of affected children live past their first year. The condition occurs in approximately 1 in 5,000 live births, with about 80% of affected newborns being female. While women of all ages can have a child with Trisomy 18, the likelihood increases with maternal age. Symptoms of Edwards Syndrome The clinical features of Edwards syndrome include: Clenched hands Crossed legs, which is often the preferred position Feet with a rounded bottom, also referred to as rocker-bottom feet Low birth weight Low-set ears Intellectual disability A small jaw (micrognathia) Underdeveloped fingernails Undescended testicles in males An unusually shaped chest, such as pectus carinatum (protruding chest) Genetics and Inheritance Most cases of Trisomy 18 result from the presence of three copies of chromosome 18 in every cell of the body, rather than the usual two. This extra genetic material disrupts normal development, leading to the characteristic features of the condition. In approximately 5% of cases, the extra copy of chromosome 18 is present in only some of the body’s cells, a condition known as mosaic Trisomy 18. The severity of mosaic Trisomy 18 depends on the type and number of cells with the extra chromosome. Development in individuals with mosaic Trisomy 18 can range from normal to severely affected. In rare cases, the long arm (q arm) of chromosome 18 may become attached (translocated) to another chromosome during the formation of reproductive cells (eggs or sperm) or early in embryonic development. Individuals with this form of the condition, known as translocation Trisomy 18, have two normal copies of chromosome 18, along with extra material from chromosome 18 attached to another chromosome. If only part of the q arm is present in three copies, the physical signs may differ from those typically seen in Trisomy 18. If the entire q arm is present in three copies, the individual may be as severely affected as those with three full copies of chromosome 18. Most cases of Trisomy 18 are not inherited but occur as random events during the formation of eggs and sperm. An error in cell division, known as nondisjunction, results in a reproductive cell with an abnormal number of chromosomes. For example, an egg or sperm cell may gain an extra copy of chromosome 18. If one of these atypical reproductive cells contributes to the genetic makeup of a child, the child will have an extra chromosome 18 in all of their cells. Mosaic Trisomy 18 is also not inherited and occurs as a random event during cell division early in embryonic development. As a result, some cells in the body have the usual two copies of chromosome 18, while others have three copies. Translocation Trisomy 18, however, can be inherited. An unaffected individual may carry a rearrangement of genetic material between chromosome 18 and another chromosome, known as a balanced translocation, because there is no extra material from chromosome 18. Although these individuals do not exhibit signs of Trisomy 18, they are at an increased risk of having children with the condition. When to Seek Medical Care If you have had a child with Trisomy 18 and are planning to have another child, it is important to consult with your healthcare provider and a genetic counselor. Genetic counseling can help families understand the condition, assess the risks of inheritance, and provide guidance on caring for the patient. Diagnosis During pregnancy, an unusually large uterus and excess amniotic fluid may be detected. After birth, the placenta may appear unusually small. Physical examination of the infant may reveal unique fingerprint patterns, and X-rays may show a short breastbone. Chromosome studies can confirm the presence of Trisomy 18, partial Trisomy, or translocation. Additional findings may include: A hole, split, or cleft in the iris (coloboma) Separation between the left and right sides of the rectus abdominis muscle (diastasis recti) Umbilical or inguinal hernia Congenital heart defects are common and may include: Atrial septal defect (ASD) Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) Ventricular septal defect (VSD) Kidney abnormalities may also be present, such as: Horseshoe kidney Hydronephrosis Polycystic kidney Treatment Options The treatment of children with Trisomy 18 is individualized and planned on a case-by-case basis, depending on the specific medical needs of the patient. Prevention Prenatal diagnosis of Trisomy 18 is possible through procedures such as amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling, combined with chromosome studies on amniotic cells. Parents who have a child with translocational Trisomy 18 and wish to have additional children should undergo chromosome studies, as they may be at an increased risk of having another child with Trisomy 18. Prognosis The prognosis for infants with Trisomy 18 is poor. Approximately 50% of affected infants do not survive beyond the first week of life. While some children have survived into their teenage years, they typically experience severe medical and developmental challenges.
